articles.title: What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?
articles.summary: The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

image.caption: Delegations from Russia and Ukraine held US-mediated talks in Abu DhabiImage: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.
The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."
How significant is the prisoner swap?
Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.
"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."
A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.
Russia, Ukraine exchange prisoners as talks end
Empty diplomacy without a real breakthrough?

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.
Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."
Experts: chances for Russia-Ukraine ceasefire low as things currently stand

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.
Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

blocks.caption: Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, briefed journalists during the talks between Russia and UkraineImage: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Redrawing borders to make Putin feel like a winner?

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."
Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.
"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.
Putin demands large swaths of Ukrainian territory

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.
"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.
Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it?
Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.
What next after Abu Dhabi?

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.
Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit
articles.summary:
Swedish activist criticised world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown

The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg, who…

blocks.text: The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg, who excoriated world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown in her first appearance at the annual UN climate talks in five years.

Thunberg, 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis.
“It [Earth] is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg said.

“No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.”

Thunberg, who in recent years has shifted her focus towards other areas such as the conflict in Gaza, linked worsening global heating to other calamities such as war in an appearance alongside activists from Nepal, Canada and Australia.
“We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” she said.
“It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.”

The intervention, on the fourth day of the two-week summit, came as world leaders who travelled to the Mediterranean coastal city delivered their own verdicts on the climate crisis and the faltering progress to address it.
Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, who was the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said in a speech that the record hot summer in the UK was “not normal”.

“The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” said Burnham, who promised the UK would get to net zero emissions, and backed a proposal for countries to further electrify their economies.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said the climate crisis was ‘upon us now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere’.  Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

blocks.text: Beth John, a climate justice adviser at Oxfam GB, said Burnham’s appearance “sends a positive signal”. But she added: “Showing up is not enough: a crisis of this scale needs substantive action, not just signals. The real test of climate leadership is delivery, not declarations.”

The electrification goal is one of the main potential promises expected at the talks, which are being jointly presided over by Turkey and Australia. Some countries want the agreement text to specify that the electricity will be derived from clean energy sources.
Campaigners have criticised governments for their slow pace of emissions cuts and for, so far, failing to rally around a phaseout of fossil fuels in the negotiations.

Current policies are set to heat the planet by 2.7C by the end of the century, a report by Climate Action Tracker found on Thursday. The catastrophic rise in temperatures is slightly more than the group expected last year and well above the 1.5C that world leaders have promised.

blocks.caption: ‘We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,’ said Nepal’s environment minister of the flash floods and landslides in the Nuwakot district in August. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Thursday was rife with accounts of the harm caused by the climate crisis. Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s environment minister, recounted the disastrous landslide that struck the country in August due to a melting glacier, claiming more than 1,500 lives.
after newsletter promotion

“We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,” Chaudhary told the Guardian. “We lost people, we lost lives, we lost property. Nepal is working for rehabilitation, reconstruction and rebuilding the infrastructure. But the communities, the culture, the lives, we cannot revive.”

In the main conference room, a speech by Mohammad Mustafa, the prime minister of Palestine, drew a standing ovation from delegates as he described the environmental impact of the three-year war with Israel.

“Israel’s restrictions on access to land, water and natural resources have compounded Palestine’s climate challenges,” said Mustafa, who said widespread destruction in Gaza, including to water, sewage and farmland, had worsened environmental and health risks.

The Turkish hosts of Cop31 have repeatedly accused Israel of genocide and refused to invite the country’s leadership to Antalya. Israel denies that it has committed genocide and insists it has fought a legitimate war to safeguard its own security.

blocks.caption: John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, said Donald Trump was ‘the biggest loser we’ve seen for a long time’ on climate issues.  Photograph: Kaan Soyturk/Reuters

blocks.text: Another country not formally present at the talks is the US, which did not send a delegation. Donald Trump has withdrawn the country from the international climate framework, derided climate science as a “hoax”, and claimed he would not permit any new wind turbines.

This stance earned a rebuke from John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, who has made the trip to Turkey along with 20 Democratic members of Congress and two state governors. “He’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues,” Kerry said of Trump in response to a question from the Guardian.

blocks.caption: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, warned that the Trump administration would ‘double down’ in the remaining presidential term.  Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters

blocks.text: The crushing midterm election win by the Democrats has raised hopes here at Cop of the US re-engaging on the climate crisis. But Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, warned the final two years of the Trump presidency would not see fundamental change on climate policy.
“I don’t want to romanticise what this will mean,” Newsom said on Thursday. “I don’t expect they’ll do anything but double down.”

articles.title: UK car industry to press EU for two-year delay to Brexit EV tariffs
articles.summary: ‘Rules of origin’ on vehicle batteries due to come into force on 1 January if deal on new delay is not reached

blocks.text: The UK car industry is preparing to push for a two-year delay to Brexit tariffs on electric cars traded with the EU, after an initial European proposal suggested a shorter delay.

Tariffs are due to kick in on 1 January for the majority of electric cars traded between the EU and UK unless the two sides can come to an agreement to delay for a second time the implementation of “rules of origin” on batteries.

The Brexit deal, rushed through on Christmas Eve in 2020, included a clause that British and European electric cars would have to use batteries made in either the UK or the EU with local materials, or face 10% tariffs. The rules would not have existed had the UK remained in the EU.

The rules were initially due to come into force on 1 January 2024, encouraging the industry to invest in local lithium-ion battery manufacturing rather than relying on the dominant Chinese battery industry. In 2020 the prospects seemed rosy, but three years later several prominent projects on both sides of the Channel had collapsed. The EU and UK agreed to extend the deadline in December 2023.

Other battery projects have since taken their place, but many are yet to produce at the scale required to meet European demand. Instead, carmakers are mainly reliant on imports from China, Japan and South Korea.

blocks.caption: Workers at an AESC battery manufacturing plant in Sunderland. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Guardian

blocks.text: Carmakers in the UK and Europe are united in their calls for the introduction of the rules of origin to be delayed again. However, an agreement has yet to be reached, with the EU and UK also wrangling over whether Britain can be included in “Made in Europe” subsidies, and whether the UK should match EU tariffs on Chinese car imports. The topics are likely to form part of an EU-UK summit planned for next week.

The European Commission has shared proposals with the automotive industry to delay the start of the tariffs, although they have not yet been shared formally with the UK government. The proposals are understood to be highly technical, but essentially equate to delaying the start of the rules of origin by a year.
Some of the proposals are understood to include adjusting customs procedures and origin calculation methodologies, which could offer some temporary tariff flexibility.
after newsletter promotion
However, some parts of the UK car industry believe more time is needed for the sector to adapt and for battery gigafactories to churn out enough units.

One executive in the UK said: “The industry will be really clear – two years minimum or we have the same discussion next year. Giga-industrialisation is happening in the EU and UK but it is not producing at the required volume yet.”
Another person said the negotiations would also focus on the technical details of the proposals, rather than simply aiming for a set time delay.

The European Automobile Manufacturers Association, an influential lobby group in Brussels, has argued that the tariffs are a serious concern for Europe’s automotive industry. It estimated that 82% of EU electric car and van exports to the UK would face the 10% customs duty in 2027 under the rules, adding costs of €1.47bn (£1.23bn) next year alone.

articles.title: Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul
articles.summary: The reforms mark a break the the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial "heartbeat regulation" is to be scrapped and women are to be better protected against violence.

image.caption: Peter Magyar said the heartbeat regulation had not led to a decline in pregnanciesImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.
Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.
Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.
The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.
The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.
Hungary to end controversial 'fetal heartbeat' policy

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.
The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.
The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."
The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.
What is the Istanbul Convention?

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.
"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar said.
The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."
"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.
Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

articles.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
articles.summary: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in both Washington and Beijing, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.
The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into free fall this week, undone by romantic entanglements, that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman, alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.
His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips, which are used to power the new technology.
The company, which is still valued at nearly $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang has had access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President XI Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn (£109bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work at their father's firm.
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan, he has a reputation for having incredibly high standards for his staff.

The company became a key provider of computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in direction and entered the world of AI. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At a recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Huang and Musk.
It was no surprise that Huang was at the top table. Companies using Nvidia's chips include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.
In essence, Huang's customer base includes the biggest firms on the planet and they are spending plenty on Nvidia's products.
This intertwining of companies means that the negative impact being felt by Nvidia, on the stock market for example, could perhaps have wider implications on other companies and the wider economy.
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, and that it was "very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, had backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

articles.title: ‘Resetting BSKE no longer in Comelec’s hands’
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections can no longer set a new date for the postponed barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) originally scheduled for Nov. 2, leaving Congress to determine when the…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) can no longer set a new date for the postponed barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) originally scheduled for Nov. 2, leaving Congress to determine when the polls will be held.
In an interview, Comelec Chairman George Garcia said the poll body may reschedule elections within 30 days only if the postponement is declared before the scheduled election day.

He made the clarification following election lawyer Romulo Macalintal’s motion for partial reconsideration of the Supreme Court ruling upholding the constitutionality of Republic Act 12326, which extends the terms of barangay officials to five years and sets the next BSKE on Nov. 13, 2028.
Garcia said that even if the Supreme Court reverses its earlier ruling, the Comelec may no longer have the authority to set a new date for the postponed elections.

“Under the law, if an election is postponed before the scheduled election day, we may set a new date, provided that it does not exceed 30 days from the original schedule,” he said. “However, once the scheduled election day has passed, even if a decision is issued, the Comelec may no longer have the authority to set a new date.”
He said Congress would have to determine the new election schedule if the Supreme Court reverses its decision.
‘No-el in 2028 unlikely’
Meanwhile, lawyer Ralph Sarmiento, who specializes in constitutional law, said postponing the national elections in 2028 will be unlikely following the deferment of the BSKE.
He pointed out that the 1987 Constitution has fixed the schedule of the election of national officials.

“Technically, it is highly likely that postponement will not happen with respect to the presidential and national elections because there are clearer provisions in our Constitution,” he said in an interview on The STAR’s online show “Truth on the Line.”

The Constitution declares that election for president, vice president, senator and member of the House of Representatives “shall be held on the second Monday of May,” with one term of six years for president and vice president, two terms of six years each for senator, and three terms of three years each for member of the House.
Previously, Macalintal expressed fear that a no-election or “no-el” scenario might happen, warning that lawmakers may also move to defer the May 2028 national elections.
Garcia said the Comelec is preparing for the next BSKE scheduled for Nov. 13, 2028, giving assurance that election materials procured for the postponed polls have been properly secured.
He said the commission had arranged with suppliers to safeguard election materials, including pens and indelible ink, and ensure their replacement in case of damage.
On voter registration, Garcia expressed confidence that the Comelec would surpass its target of registering three million voters for the 2028 elections.
Nearly 37,000 people registered nationwide on the first day of the registration period, with the number reaching almost 80,000 in the first two days, Garcia said.
He noted that registration turnout remained high on the third day, with some registration centers, including those in shopping malls, struggling to accommodate applicants before closing time.
He attributed the turnout partly to the participation of young Filipinos, particularly those aged 17 and 18, as well as applicants seeking to transfer their registration.
Garcia also cited the demand for voter certification, which the Comelec now provides for free, as another factor drawing applicants to registration centers.– Ghio Ong

articles.title: AMLC: No flood control money in Martin’s accounts
articles.summary: An investigator of the Anti-Money Laundering Council told the Sandiganbayan that the AMLC found no record of contractors, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), or former lawmaker Zaldy…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — An investigator of the Anti-Money Laundering Council told the Sandiganbayan that the AMLC found no record of contractors, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), or former lawmaker Zaldy Co sending money to suspended Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez when he was House speaker.

AMLC financial investigator Jan Mark Busa, who testified in Romualdez’s bail hearing, told the court that the P560.5 million worth of remittances that went to the bank account of the Leyte lawmaker were not related to flood control transactions or unlawful activities.

During the cross-examination of defense counsel Rashel Ann Pomoy, Busa said the AMLC examined 35 accounts associated with Romualdez and monitored P560.5 million worth of bank transactions from September 2022 to March 2025.
Asked if it would be correct that the AMLC did not have findings that these transactions were related to flood control projects, Busa answered in the affirmative.
The investigation, Busa said, covered 1,951 financial transactions of Romualdez from 2022 to 2025.
He also said there “appears to be a huge disparity” between the inflow of money in Romualdez’s accounts and the P7.4-billion plundered money alleged by ombudsman prosecutors.
Busa also testified that there was no AMLC record of Romualdez sending money to Golden Pheasant, the company allegedly used by the lawmaker to purchase a property in South Forbes Park in Makati City.
Moreover, there are no records of Romualdez sending money to OMLAW, Samchan or lawyer Jose Paras.
Judge scolds BJMP over changing testimony

Third Division chairperson Associate Justice Karl Miranda scolded a Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) warden over inconsistencies in her testimony on the access granted to Romualdez’s personal staff at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.

During the bail hearing, Supt. Maria Lourdes Pacion said that Romualdez’s personal staff, Arvin de Guzman, was allowed to set up the lawmaker’s CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine at night.

Miranda, however, pointed out that this is contrary to Pacion’s earlier testimony that De Guzman was only allowed inside the facility during visiting hours, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., although exceeding at times.
“You’re here to tell us the truth. Stop changing the story. Just stick to one, which is the truth,” Miranda said.

Pacion said she allowed De Guzman to assist with the CPAP machine because Romualdez was not mentally stable and required continued medical care, which includes regular blood pressure monitoring, uninterrupted access and compliance with his prescribed medications, and consistent nightly use of the breathing apparatus.
However, Miranda said it seems the BJMP is giving special consideration to Romualdez by allowing him a personal assistant. Miranda said it should be the BJMP personnel attending to Romualdez’s needs.
DOJ: Over P866 million in flood money returned
More than P866 million allegedly stolen from anomalous flood control projects have been recovered by the government, the Department of Justice (DOJ) reported.
A total of P866,381,500 has been “returned to the DOJ and deposited to the Bureau of Treasury,” the agency said in its one-year accomplishment report yesterday.
The current total increased by P25 million from the P841,381,500 restituted amount last July.
It did not provide a breakdown of where the funds came from.

However, DOJ Senior Undersecretary Raul Vasquez noted that “the last one came from Henry Alcantara,” which he said was given in “cold cash,” while restitution by former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) undersecretary Roberto Bernardo was “continuous.” – Ghio Ong

MANILA, Philippines — Hollywood actress and humanitarian advocate Angelina Jolie has called for greater investment in vulnerable communities, saying only genuine development can make them self-sufficient and less dependent on external assistance.

Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Inclusive Growth Summit on Wednesday, Jolie said humanitarian assistance should be more than providing immediate relief, as it should aim for creating long-term opportunities in education, livelihood and economic development.

articles.title: Marcos calls for patience amid ASEAN Summit disruptions
articles.summary: As monstrous traffic jams hit Metro Manila and flights were slated for cancellation or rescheduling, President Marcos yesterday called for cooperation and appealed for patience for the inconveniences…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am
Philippines launches ASEAN chairship Pres. Ferdinand Marcos Jr. leads the launch of the Philippines' chairship of ASEAN 2026 in Intramuros, Manila on November 14, 2025.
RTV Malacañang / Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — As monstrous traffic jams hit Metro Manila and flights were slated for cancellation or rescheduling, President Marcos yesterday called for cooperation and appealed for patience for the inconveniences caused by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

In a vlog entry posted on YouTube, Marcos said the summit is crucial as the Philippines and the rest of the world grapple with a number of challenges like the rising prices of fuel and goods, the economic slowdown, the El Niño phenomenon and security issues.

“We cannot solve many of these problems by ourselves so ASEAN is really important... As the host of the 49th ASEAN Summit, we have a huge opportunity to lead the crafting of the agenda and prioritize issues that are important to our countrymen like fuel prices, food security, agriculture, jobs and livelihood,” he said.
According to Marcos, it is a huge honor to host the ASEAN Summit, which he described as a good opportunity to showcase the beauty of the Philippines and the skill of the Filipinos.
“The preparations have been finalized and they are detailed. The skill and creativity of Filipinos will surely be highlighted,” the President said.

“Although some will experience inconvenience in the succeeding days, it will be temporary and we ask for a little patience. I am sure that they will be outweighed by the benefits we will attain from the policies to be agreed upon and the jobs to be created,” he added.

Authorities are set to enforce a security exclusion zone within the parameter of the Philippine International Convention Center, the venue of the event, from Nov. 15 to 18. Although there will be no general road closures during the duration of the summit, a stop-and-go scheme will be implemented in some areas. The government has also provided financial aid to workers and small businesses affected by the event.
Gov’t ready for audit

As some sectors criticize the costs of the Philippines’ hosting of ASEAN, Palace press officer Claire Castro said the administration is prepared to subject its expenditures to an audit to prove that the funds are used properly.

She said P22.9 billion has been allocated for the summit but clarified that the amount has not been fully spent. “Regardless of the amount spent, we will report it. We cannot provide a final report or accounting yet because the ASEAN Summit is not yet over,” Castro said. “The government is ready to be audited.”

Meanwhile, the Philippine National Police is strengthening security at major transport hubs and tourist destinations ahead of an expected surge in travelers during the extended holiday break from Nov. 14 to 18, which coincides with the country’s hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

In anticipation of increased movements at Ninoy Aquino International Airport and other major airports in the country for the summit, Philippine Airlines announced the cancellation or reschedule of some domestic and international flights.
Cebu Pacific also adjusted flight schedules in advance to minimize disruptions during the summit.

Meanwhile, the Department of Tourism has placed immersive experiential zones and Filipino encounters at the 49th ASEAN International Media Center. – Rudy Santos, Mark Ernest Villeza, Michael Punongbayan, Andrew Ronquillo, Evelyn Macairan

articles.title: 91% of Pinoys believe Asean hosting beneficial – SWS
articles.summary: Most Filipinos believe that the country’s hosting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations leaders’ summit in Manila next week will be beneficial to the Philippines, a survey…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am
In the survey, 91 percent of respondents believed that the Philippines would either benefit “much” or “very much” from the event.
STAR / Noel Pabalate

MANILA, Philippines — Most Filipinos believe that the country’s hosting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders’ summit in Manila next week will be beneficial to the Philippines, a survey conducted by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) from Sept. 21 to 27 showed.
Seventeen percent said the country would benefit “a little,” while nine percent said there would not be any benefit at all.
Leaders of the countries in the regional bloc, as well as those from several ASEAN partners like the United States, will arrive in the country next week for the summit.
Asked what issues should the Philippines prioritize as 2026 host of the ASEAN, 19 percent answered inflation and the rising prices of goods and services.

The other concerns are the West Philippine Sea (19 percent), oil price and supply (12 percent), poverty (nine percent), economic crisis (six percent), jobs and livelihood (five percent), war and conflict (four percent), crime and illegal drugs (three percent), food supply and hunger (three percent) and safety and security (two percent). Nineteen percent of the respondents answered other issues, while 15 percent said none or just refused to answer.
The survey also showed 46 percent of the Filipino respondents claiming having much trust in the regional bloc.
This comprised 14 percent who said they trust the ASEAN “very much” and another 32 percent who said they trust it “somewhat much.”

Another 21 percent either had “somewhat little” or “very little” trust in the regional bloc, with the remaining 31 percent undecided. This resulted in a net trust rating of +25, considered by SWS as “moderate.”
SWS data showed that this is lower than the +41 obtained in June 2017, composed of 56 percent who had much trust and 21 percent who had little trust in the regional bloc.
The net trust rating is obtained by subtracting those who had little trust from those who had much trust in the bloc.
The latest survey had 1,500 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent.

articles.title: Persistent China-linked dredging in Zambales hit
articles.summary: Opposition Rep. Leila de Lima again expressed exasperation over the continued large-scale dredging in Zambales, particularly the reported use of Chinese vessels, warning that the operations threaten…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am
Zambales as seen on Google Maps.
Google Maps / Philstar.com screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — Opposition Rep. Leila de Lima again expressed exasperation over the continued large-scale dredging in Zambales, particularly the reported use of Chinese vessels, warning that the operations threaten the province’s coastal environment, fishing grounds, and the livelihoods of local communities.

The senior deputy minority leader filed House Resolution 1601, seeking a congressional investigation into dredging activities in Zambales’ rivers, estuaries and coastal waters, including reports of Chinese vessels operating in the area.

“So many questions need to be answered with this really bothersome dredging in Zambales which also requires immediate action. We won’t allow this alarming issue to be ignored or left unaddressed,” the former senator and justice secretary said.

“We need to know the real truth here not just for the purpose of identifying the culprit behind the abuse, neglect or inadequacies, so that operations like these will not be repeated anymore, precisely because this threatens our Mother Earth, and livelihood of our kababayans,” De Lima said.

The Mamamayang Liberal party-list representative said the probe should establish the extent of foreign involvement in the operations, determine where the extracted materials are being brought, and identify possible violations of environmental laws.

“With large-scale dredging unabated, coastal erosion and loss of livelihoods unresolved, and questions regarding the foreign vessels involved, the volume of materials dredged and their destination still unaddressed, every day of delay in conducting an inquiry into the matter poses greater risks of further and potentially irreversible damage to coastal areas, fishing grounds, and the communities that depend on them,” De Lima warned.

She also called for stronger safeguards, transparency mechanisms, and accountability measures to ensure that dredging and reclamation activities do not come at the expense of the environment and affected communities.

The lawmaker’s renewed push comes amid persistent complaints from environmental groups, including the Zambales Ecological Network, Save Our Shores Zambales, and the Institute for Area Management, which have questioned whether supposed flood control and river restoration projects are being used to facilitate large-scale sand mining and extraction.

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources issued Administrative Order 2019-13 in October 2019, establishing exclusive dredging zones in heavily silted river systems, particularly the Bucao, Maloma and Sto. Tomas rivers in Zambales.

articles.title: AMLC gets CA asset freeze order covering lawmaker, ex-official
articles.summary: The Anti-Money Laundering Council has secured a freeze order from the Court of Appeals covering bank accounts and other properties of a lawmaker and a former government official over alleged…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am
This photo shows the Anti-Money Laundering Council seal.
Philstar.com illustration

MANILA, Philippines — The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) has secured a freeze order from the Court of Appeals covering bank accounts and other properties of a lawmaker and a former government official over alleged corruption involving government contracts.
In a statement yesterday, the AMLC said the appellate court issued the freeze order on Nov. 9 against the lawmaker and a businessman who previously held public office.
A freeze order temporarily prevents the withdrawal, transfer or disposal of covered assets suspected to be linked to unlawful activities. It does not constitute a finding of guilt.
The AMLC did not disclose the identities of the individuals or the value of the assets covered by the order.
The petition stemmed from a complaint filed by the Office of the Ombudsman against the two individuals for alleged violations of the Plunder Law and the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
“The complaint is based on the alleged grant of exclusive contracts to corporations associated with the lawmaker during the businessman’s tenure in government,” the AMLC said.

According to the AMLC, its investigation uncovered extensive fund transfers between the lawmaker’s personal bank accounts and those of the corporations, establishing a financial connection between the parties.

Investigators also discovered substantial and complex transactions involving the businessman, whose financial activity increased significantly during the period when numerous contracts were awarded to companies linked to the lawmaker.
The Court of Appeals found probable cause to believe that the lawmaker may have benefited financially from the alleged unlawful activities.

The court also found probable cause to believe that the businessman participated in the alleged wrongdoing, citing his involvement in awarding the contracts and the increase in his financial transactions.
Separately, the AMLC said it filed a petition for civil forfeiture on Oct. 23 involving assets allegedly linked to another prominent legislator facing plunder charges.

The case involved alleged commissions, kickbacks and other benefits from government flood-control and infrastructure projects, which were reportedly concealed and invested through corporate entities and financial intermediaries.
Civil forfeiture is a legal process through which authorities seek the recovery of assets allegedly connected to unlawful activities.

“The AMLC is committed to combating corruption and will continue to work closely with its partner agencies in pursuing the recovery of assets that may be linked to unlawful activities, in accordance with the law,” it said.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal and is replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis – follow live
articles.summary:
Nvidia shares plunge 10% in pre-market trading after board ousts longtime boss Huang over two affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, in big blow to AI boom

Too big – and…
articles.byline: Tom Ambrose (now); Julia Kollewe and Jonathan Yerushalmy (earlier)

blocks.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal, replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis
Nvidia’s long-time boss Jensen Huang has stepped down over the scandal, and the company has appointed finance chief Colette Kress as interim chief executive.
The company issued this statement just now, after its board met last night:

double quotation markThe Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately. Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

blocks.caption: This screengrab from video footage by CTI obtained via AFPTV on 9 November shows Alice Huang (C partially obscured), a Chinese executive linked to the data centre company called Megaspeed, attending a dinner hosted by Nvidia's chief executive and co-founder Jensen Huang (R in black) at a restaura…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1h agoNvidia's value has slumped by $888bn this week
2h agoNvidia shares now down 10% in premarket trading
2h agoNvidia shares plunge 10%; board pays tribute to Huang and appoints first-ever chair
2h agoNvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over scandal, replaced by CFO Colette Kress on interim basis
2h agoUS trade representative says US 'remains concerned' about Nvidia
3h agoWall Street to open lower with tech shares seen sliding
3h agoChinese AI companies rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity
3h agoMegaspeed says 'committed to working constructively and transparently with US government'
8h agoWho could potentially replace Jensen Huang if Nvidia ousts him?
9h agoNvidia shares plunge nearly 9% in pre-market trading, reverberating across Asian markets
11h agoOpinion: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish
12h agoWhy is Nvidia so important to the AI sector?
13h agoHow did we get here?
14h agoNvidia share price plunges 8% in after-hours trade
14h agoJensen Huang's future rests in the balance as Nvidia board reportedly meet

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, has said that investors have been left “concerned” over the change of leadership at Nvidia.
She said that although the interim appointment of Colette Kress will “provide continuity” for the firm, it remains to be seen if Nvidia will be able to keep pace with its rivals.
Hathorn said:

double quotation markThe main concern for investors is the uncertainty following a change of leadership, especially one with a lack of planning like this one. However, the key-man risk is significant, but it shouldn’t be confused with the company’s entire investment case. Huang has been instrumental in Nvidia’s transformation into the dominant supplier of AI computing infrastructure, and his departure creates uncertainty around strategy, execution and relationships with major customers. But Nvidia’s technological advantages, CUDA software ecosystem and substantial order book do not disappear with its CEO. The appointment of CFO Colette Kress provides some continuity, although investors will want reassurance that the broader leadership team can maintain Nvidia’s pace of innovation and defend its market position.

She added that Nvidia’s recovery today “looks partly driven by bargain hunting after an aggressive selloff, with some investors seemingly betting that Nvidia’s competitive advantages, strong AI demand and established customer relationships will survive a leadership transition.”
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at the the UK’s largest non-advisory investment service Wealth Club, said Nvidia’s board “clearly wanted to disassociate with Jensen Huang”.
In analysis earlier today, she said:

double quotation markEven Jensen Huang’s superstar status could not eclipse the deep damage the scandal has wreaked on the Nvidia’s reputation. Even tech icons of his stature are not immune to being acountable to corporate responsibility. The emergence of the second affair, this one rumoured to be with an employee, appears to have been the last straw for the board. With the firm facing so many investigations – launched by the FBI and from Capitol hill, the board clearly wants to disassociate the company from Huang’s actions as much as possible.
Streeter added that interim CEO Colette Kress is “seen as a safe pair of hands” and that she has “clearly been brought in to steady the ship”.
However, she warned:

double quotation markBut she lacks global status and is unlikely to be able to forge such deep global commercial ties as Nvidia is set to enter into a period of uncertainty over strategic priorities, pricing, supply agreements and future product commitments. Nvidia has lost a strategic visionary, and it’s set to have repercussions right through the AI trade, given how the chip giant is right at the heart of this technological revolution.
Nvidia’s shares are recovering from that early tumble – they’re down ‘only’ 7.7% – which knocks around $320bn off its valuation.
Nvidia's value has slumped by $888bn this week

blocks.caption: Graeme Wearden

blocks.text: Graeme Wearden
More than $575bn has been wiped off Nvidia’s value at the start of trading, as investors react to the departure of Jensen Huang.
Nvidia’s shares have tumbled by over 13% at the start of trading, dropping to $149.79 from $173.73 last night.
They ended last week at $186.64 each. And (by my maths), the company’s valuation has now slumped by $888bn so far this week.
Having ended Friday night worth $4.5tn, Nvidia’s value has now dropped to $3.61bn.
In China, 888 is seen as a lucky number... but not for Huang or Nvidia.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson in Portland, Oregon, has looked at the new interim CEO of Nvidia, Colette Kress, who will also continue to serve as chief financial officer.
Luria told Reuters:

double quotation markColette Kress is well respected by investors and should be able to guide Nvidia through this challenging period. The task is daunting, as Nvidia has been founder-led since inception and Mr Huang concentrated much of the decision making.
Ben Barringer, head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said:

double quotation markJensen Huang clearly saw the writing was on the wall and has made the decision to resign as chief executive of Nvidia. This is an important moment in broader financial markets due to the clout that Huang carried, and the fact he had developed Nvidia into the most valuable and influential company in the world. It remains to be seen if Huang will eventually stick around in some sort of ceremonial or non-executive capacity. It would be difficult to see him not retaining some sort of influence over Nvidia, but we do not yet know the full details of the allegations or the outcome of the investigation, and much of what happens next still depends on that. For now, CFO Colette Kress has taken the role on an interim position. While there is no natural successor in place, she is the most obvious internal candidate and will now likely use this time to prove she deserves it full time. She certainly knows the company inside out and has helped develop what is a hugely successful strategy. This doesn’t necessarily harm Nvidia in the short-term. Orders remain strong and the company has a robust earnings outlook. What this news threatens to do is harm the wider AI ecosystem in the longer-term. Huang is hugely influential in the debates around AI regulation and has developed Nvidia into the leader in AI investment and financing. With his voice now removed from the table, and the potential for Nvidia to pivot on its strategy over time, the company may not carry the sway it once did.
Turning to the wider outlook for technology firms, he said:

double quotation markThis news ultimately pours petrol onto what is already a volatile picture for tech companies following the midterm elections. Nvidia and its neocloud partners are likely to bear the initial brunt of this news, while competitors like AMD and Broadcom benefit. That said, this news has the potential to be game changing over the long-term with a key figure out of the picture.
Jensen Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priemand “with a vision to bring 3D graphics to the gaming and multimedia markets”.
Huang is the company’s fourth-largest investor with a ⁠stake of about 3.61% and will not ⁠remain on the board.
Here’s some instant reaction to his departure.

Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional investor content at Morningstar, says governance issues and succession planning, long neglected at Nvidia, will become important for other founder-led companies.

double quotation markThe sudden departure of one of the world’s most influential CEOs illustrates just how quickly an unconventional governance structure can become a source of risk, and often real losses, for investors. While Nvidia’s share price rocketed over the last few years, very few people were asking deep questions about CEO succession planning, board composition and challenge, or oversight of geopolitically sensitive aspects of company strategy. Now, all those issues will be front and centre, perhaps not just for Nvidia, but also for other founder-led companies like Anthropic, Meta Platforms and SpaceX.
Nvidia shares now down 10% in premarket trading
Nvidia’s shares are falling deeper into the red in pre-market trading, ahead of the open of Wall Street in less than 25 minutes.
They were already heading for a fall, as investors were unsettled by the news that Nvidia’s board had met last night to consider Jensen Huang’s future.
Now that he has resigned, Nvidia’s shares are down 10.4% – an indication of how trading may proceed when the New York stock market session begins.
Nvidia shares plunge 10%; board pays tribute to Huang and appoints first-ever chair
Nvidia shares have plummeted 10% on the news!
Nvidia paid tribute to Huang, saying:

double quotation markJensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

Kress, the new interim chief executive, has served as executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia since joining the company in September 2013. The group said she has played a key role in Nvidia’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The Nvidia board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as chief efficer and executive chairman of Synopsys.
Jones said:

double quotation markColette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position. She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.
Kress said:

double quotation markNvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years. We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.
The US chipmaker will report its third-quarter results on 17 November.
US trade representative says US 'remains concerned' about Nvidia

US trade representative Jamieson ⁠Greer ⁠said ⁠the United States “remains ⁠concerned” ​about the tech giant ‌Nvidia, ‌as the world’s ‌dominant supplier of AI chips grapples with fallout ‌from reports of two extramarital ​affairs involving its longtime ⁠chief executive Jensen Huang.
Greer told CNBC ​on Thursday:
double quotation markObviously we ​remain concerned.
Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese businesswoman and former Megaspeed executive, who is accused of spying for Beijing. She has reportedly returned to China.
Wall Street to open lower with tech shares seen sliding
Wall Street is expected to have a bumpy start in just over an hour, with technology shares likely to slide again as the scandal around Nvidia boss Jensen Huang deepens.
Stock futures are extending losses, with the S&P 500 down 0.75%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 1.5% lower and Dow Jones down 0.2%.
Also, Donald Trump said: “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”
In the second half of a post about corruption in the US, on the social media platform Truth Social, he said:

double quotation markWe don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DJT
Oil prices have see-sawed today. Brent crude is now trading 1.5% higher at $93.98 a barrel.
Gold prices have also fallen, by about 2%.

articles.title: Sri Lanka: Rights groups sound alarm over proposed anti-terror law
articles.summary: The Sri Lankan government is looking to replace a controversial anti-terror law but critics say the new one is just as bad.

image.caption: The government argues a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex activities of extremist groupsImage: Eranga Jayawardane/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For 46-year-old Ganesan (name changed) from Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, any discussion of terrorism brings back memories of his two-year-old daughter, who was killed in the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks. She was one of 270 people who lost their lives in a series of coordinated bombings targeting three churches and three luxury hotels across the island nation.
The attacks were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Over 500 people were injured.
Ganesan's daughter was killed in an attack on the Zion Church in Batticaloa.
But Ganesan remains skeptical when asked about the new counterterrorism bill pushed by the government in Sri Lanka.
"Laws against terrorism are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks, but they should not target the innocent or suppress human rights," he told DW.
The administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his National People's Power faction

has proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) as a replacement for the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). The PTA has many critics who claim that the contentious law has enabled arbitrary detention and the torture of detainees for decades.
The government argues that a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex local and international activities of extremist groups.
What do rights groups say about the new bill?

But rights groups are now also sharply criticizing the new bill. Activist argue that the changes will not bring about any improvement, warning that the draft features an overly broad definition of terrorism, provides inadequate judicial oversight, and grants extensive powers to law enforcement authorities. Activists also warn that the proposed law has only limited safeguards against official abuse.

The bill, for instance, allows security forces to stop, search and question individuals on the basis of "reasonable suspicion," enter and search premises, and seize items on suspicion of them being linked to an offense under the terrorism act.

blocks.caption: President Anura Kumara Dissanayake's government is replacing the contentious Prevention of Terrorism Act [FILE: September 22, 2024]Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: "The definition of the term 'terrorism' in the bill as presently drafted is highly problematic. The term is unclear, and its meaning has not been clearly defined," Visakesa Chandrasekaram, a film director and human rights lawyer, told DW.
"Such lack of clarity in the law may result in violations of the fundamental rights of the people," he added.

Chandrasekaram also pointed out that the bill would confer police powers on the military, which is neither trained to investigate criminal offenses nor equipped to protect the rights of people targeted in such investigations.
This, he warned, could lead to the "militarization" of the law enforcement process.
Is the new law just PTA all over again?
Dhanushka Silva, a lawyer, said the proposed law is not much different from the existing one.
"The present government pledged to repeal the PTA in their 2024 election manifesto. But now the government seems to replace it with a new act that is a replica of the PTA," he told DW.
Silva believes the new bill, PSTA, could be misused to suppress democratic freedoms and muzzle dissent and free speech.
Under Section 9 of the PSTA, even posts or statements made on social media could be subject to scrutiny due to the broad definition of terrorism-related offenses in the bill, he explained.
The section further suggests that individuals who share content deemed to be a terrorism offense could face up to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, according to the the lawyer.
"This is a big blow to freedom of speech in a democratic society like ours," he said.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has also called on the government to ensure that the bill is consistent with international human rights law.
It noted that the PSTA, despite containing some additional safeguards and improvements on previous drafts, reproduces a number of shortcomings in the PTA and other, older counter-terrorism bills.
The legislation "should include robust safeguards against torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance and coercive interrogation," it said in a statement.
Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa, however, rejected the allegations by rights activists and insisted that the new law would not compromise civil liberties and press freedom.

blocks.caption: The 2019 Easter Sunday attacks targeted three churches and three luxury hotels across Sri Lanka [FILE: April 21, 2020]Image: Eranga Jayawardena/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Calls for Colombo to uphold human rights commitments
Passing the new counterterrorism legislation could also have economic and foreign policy ramifications for Sri Lanka.
The United Nations, which has repeatedly urged Colombo to repeal the PTA, has called for further revisions to the proposed PSTA.

The European Union has likewise urged Sri Lanka to uphold its international human rights obligations if it wishes to continue benefiting from the bloc's Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+), which grants preferential access to the EU market to eligible developing countries.
Failure to meet these requirements could result in the suspension of GSP+ preferences, likely to trigger significant economic penalties for the country.
During a parliamentary debate on November 12, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne said that some provisions of the proposed law were inconsistent with the constitution.
The legislation was also challenged before the Supreme Court, which outlined several amendments and said Parliament could pass the measure once the changes were made.
Parliament has yet to set a date for a vote.

articles.title: Chua likens BPI witness to opening Pandora's box for defense
articles.summary: The defense team decided against fielding a witness from the BPI because there was no guarantee their testimony would favor the Vice President, the House prosecution panel said.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 11:31pm

The House prosecution panel at the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte speculated that the defense team decided against fielding a witness from the BPI because there was no guarantee that the testimony would favor her.

The defense decided to dispense with the testimony of Paul Roderick Ysmael, BPI senior vice president of, saying it was already established that Poa wrote a letter to the BPI about the bank accounts of the Vice President and her husband, Manases Carpio.

“We have to remember that the account in BPI Julia Vargas is a key issue. That is a huge account. If this is discussed, they would have to answer our questions about that. It is like opening a Pandora’s box for them,” House prosecutors Joel Chua of Manila said in a press conference, referring to the joint account Duterte has with her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, at the BPI bank on Julia Vargas Avenue in Pasig City.

“We’re not saying that there is more to be revealed, but they would open doors for further questions [had they made the BPI official stand as a defense witness], as we have seen in the way the prosecution conducted its cross-examination,” Chua added.
The defense also earlier dropped the fielding of 15 witnesses from other banks so as not to “waste the time of the court.”
“There are avoiding a floodgate of questions that they could not possibly manage,” Chua said.

He added that without bank officials as defense witnesses, the testimony of prosecution witness and financial forensic expert Alex Cabrera, as well as the bank officials who testified on the ending balances of the bank accounts of the Vice President and her husband, will remain uncontested.

“The bank accounts of the Duterte-Carpio couple already have hundreds of million [not declared in t their Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth. On top of that, if you will recall, the AMLC likewise presented several transactions, the covered and the suspicious transactions at P4.4 billion. So far, that’s undisputed,” Chua said.

“Those are indisputable facts because the bank managers themselves have testified on those bank accounts that bear or bore certain amounts,” House prosecution team spokesperson Zia Alonto Adiong of Lanao del Sur added.

Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr., for his part, said the defense did not question the authenticity of those bank accounts of the Duterte-Carpio couple when the prosecution presented them as evidence. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists
articles.summary: A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's goverment. One was also convicted of planning a violent…

image.caption: The trial opened at Woolwich Crown Court in London on October 5 this yearImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying in dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.
The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.
What did the court rule?

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.
The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.
One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.
A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

blocks.caption: Sentencing in the case is expected at the 'Old Bailey' in London on December 17Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.
Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.
The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online
"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.
Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.
Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.
UK releases air base plot suspects
Not the first plot targeting Iran International
There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.
In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."
Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.
What other alleged signs of Iranian hostile activity in the UK are there?
British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.
Three men were indicted in the US in relation that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.
Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.
France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.
