blocks.text: Bomb alert at Calais-Fréthun train station causes delays on domestic, cross channel services
I am also keeping one eye on another bomb alert in Europe, this time at Calais-Fréthun station in northern France.

blocks.caption: A Eurostar passenger train arrives to enter the Channel Tunnel in Coquelles, northern France. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The station remains closed as the alert is getting “assessed,” local authorities said.

The disruption is having a knock on effect on French and international trains: Eurostar services to and from London are delayed as a result, with passengers warned about delays and potential further disruption.

“Due to a request for police assistance at Calais-Fréthun, your train is delayed. We’re waiting for more information and we’ll confirm your estimated delay as soon as possible. Thanks for your patience.”
I will let you know if and when we know more.
EU to approve new sanctions on Russia on Monday, France's Europe minister says
Meanwhile, the EU is planning to approve new sanctions on Russia on Monday, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said.

“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against Russia, on 150 additional entities, 50 ⁠banks and it’s France which proposed the bulk of the entities to add,” Haddad told LCI ⁠television, as reported by Reuters.
“We will continue to put economic pressure on Russia ​and of course support Ukraine,” ‌he added.

blocks.caption: France's junior minister in charge of Europe Benjamin Haddad speaks at an event this week. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images
Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are in Moscow this morning, where they are expected to meet Russia’s president Vladimir Putin to advance some of the issues discussed at trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi over the last two days.

The meeting is expected to get under way around 9am GMT, with Russia’s deputy foreign minister Sergei Rybakov trying to manage everyone’s expectations by saying it was too early to say that necessary trust had been restored between Russia and Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Russia's presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev welcoming US special envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner upon their arrival at Moscow's Vnukovo airport. Photograph: Russian Direct Investment Fund/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The US envoys are then expected to fly to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the margins of the European Political Community summit, which is being attended by more than 40 leaders from Ukraine’s allied countries.
The EPC – set up on the initiative of France’s Emmanuel Macron – offers a rare chance to discuss key European issues with non-EU allies, including Britain’s Andy Burnham and Canada’s Mark Carney.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ireland's taoiseach Micheál Martin attend a bilateral press conference at Government Buildings, in Dublin, Ireland last night. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

blocks.text: For Burnham, it’s also an opportunity to dot the i’s and cross the t’s ahead of next week’s EU-UK summit, which is a key part of his proposed reset in relationship with the bloc. Let’s see what we are going to hear on this today.
For Dublin, the meeting comes with a massive security operation, particularly after some past concerns about drones, particularly around Zelenskyy’s visit to Ireland last December.
I will keep an eye on both of these events and bring you all the latest here.
It’s Thursday, 12 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: LinkedIn, Monster take down over 1,000 fake job postings after CBC investigation
articles.summary: More than 1,500 misleading job postings on LinkedIn and Monster were actually connected to a multi-level marketing company, a CBC News visual investigation has found.
articles.byline: Eric Szeto, Courteney Dorrington, Jordan Pearson, Ivan Angelovski

image.caption: Hundreds of job postings posted to LinkedIn and Monster actually brought applicants into the recruiting process for a multi-level marketing company, a CBC News visual investigation has found. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, LinkedIn, Monster, Soho A Studio)

blocks.text: More than 1,500 misleading job postings — offering remote work, no experience needed — have been taken down from LinkedIn and Monster after a CBC visual investigation revealed the listings funnelled unsuspecting applicants to a multi-level marketing (MLM) company that asked for money.

CBC connected a network of travel-related pages posting suspicious jobs — positions like "Work From Home Travel Planner and Virtual Customer Support Representative" — to a U.S.-based MLM called Evolution Travel. Some of the roles promised to pay up to $75,000 US per year.
In reality, there was no job and no salary.

Applicants were quickly directed to join virtual information sessions, where they were asked to pay hundreds of dollars up front, followed by a monthly subscription fee. The program promised to teach members how to make money from booking travel as an independent agent and recruiting others into the program, taking a cut of their commissions.
Exposing who’s behind fake job ads online
The companies went by names like Wanderwell Collective, Professional Travel Hub, Remote-Careers, Sky Land & Ocean Travel and Sunkissed Getaways.
The job postings made no mention of Evolution Travel or sign-up fees.
Many of the jobs did not require experience and promised to pay up to $75,000 US. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC; LinkedIn)

"This is disgusting," said Jay Jones, a Chicago-based job listing investigator who CBC shared its findings with. "They catch you with the lure of the fake job. The money is great, [successful applicants] get to stay at home. You have to pay to get work — that's not how work works."
Misleading job postings — including ones that require payment or lead to MLMs — are strictly prohibited on platforms like LinkedIn and other job sites.
Jay Jones investigates misleading and fake jobs online. (CBC)

"It feels in so many ways that we're living in a funhouse mirror," said Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute, a public policy think-tank that focuses on economic resilience and digital sovereignty.
These postings risk "eroding confidence — confidence in the self and confidence that there is, frankly, meaningful work out there for people that is worth pursuing."
Jobs were 'misleading': LinkedIn

MLMs are not illegal in Canada or the U.S. However, in the U.S., companies and individuals could face fines if they are found to violate the U.S. Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits "unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce."

"I would consider [these job posts] misleading… and would invite enforcement by either the FTC, the state governments or other federal enforcement agencies," said William Kovacic, former FTC chairman and commissioner, with whom CBC also shared its findings.

One independent agent behind multiple travel businesses linked to misleading jobs ads CBC identified — Wanderwell Collective, Destination Knot, Aisle and Abroad, and Professional Travel Hub — was Diedre Norton. In one video posted to YouTube, Norton said she had a network of 300 recruits for Evolution Travel.
Even though Evolution Travel’s founder, David McCovy, praised her in online videos as being a top performer, Norton denied being affiliated with the program before hanging up on CBC News.
Screenshot of an online video showing Evolution founder David McCovy during a conference. (EvolutionTravelCafe/YouTube)
McCovy did not respond to CBC’s requests for comment.

A representative from Evolution Travel who only identified themselves by their title, chief operating officer, told CBC they have consistently told their independent agents not to post job ads on any platforms.

Late last month, LinkedIn took down close to 900 ads connected to Evolution Travel, saying it had removed them because they were "misleading and violated" company policy, adding "the companies behind them will no longer be able to post jobs" on the platform.

Monster took down 600 listings, saying it has "clear policies prohibiting misleading job postings and multi-level marketing opportunities, and we take action to remove listings that do not meet our standards."

Hundreds of job postings posted to LinkedIn and Monster actually brought applicants into the recruiting process for a multi-level marketing company, a CBC News visual investigation has found. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, LinkedIn, Monster)
Detecting fake jobs
Evolution Travel does not operate in Canada, but CBC journalists still came across the job posting in their feeds. They were also recommended in emails from LinkedIn.
The ads contained immediate red flags. The travel companies named in the ads had minimal to no presence online, and there were close to 1,500 postings, often with almost identical job descriptions.
Many of the jobs did not require experience and were remote. CBC found more than 1,500 misleading or fake jobs. (LinkedIn)
The jobs, in many cases, required no education, no prior experience and often did not require a resumé.

CBC applied for eight jobs on LinkedIn and Monster, attaching a blank document as a resumé in cases that required it. Upon applying, the team was sent automated emails to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel.
CBC journalists were sent automated emails and asked to join a virtual information session by individuals connected to Evolution Travel upon applying for the jobs. (CBC)
Evolution Travel and its partner Archer Travel Services describe themselves as an international "home-based travel business" that trains its members to book travel and earn a commission.

But it's not just about booking travel. Archer Travel’s website describes Evolution Travel as its "recruiting partner" and describes it as a "network marketing" company — another term for multi-level marketing, according to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

A compensation plan for members on Evolution Travel’s website shows a percentage of commissions and monthly bonuses are paid to the most effective recruiters, with membership tiers up to "8 Star Platinum" for recruiting 100,000 people.
Documents show compensation plans for Evolution Travel. (Evolution Travel)

None of this was mentioned in the information sessions CBC attended, which covered travel booking exclusively. When a CBC journalist posing as a job applicant asked about getting commissions from their own recruits, the session host said it was not covered in the information sessions and that the person who invited them into the program would address it.
Session hosts also didn’t disclose there is a hidden $50 annual fee in the independent contractor agreement, seen by CBC, when signing up.
A screenshot from an Evolution virtual session shows the packages attendees can pay to enrol in the program. (Evolution Travel)
Former FTC chairman and commissioner Kovacic said if he were still at the agency, he would be looking into the company.
"[Fees are] not presented in the initial interaction," he said. "It's shrouded in a way that's very important and would mislead users."
27,000 independent contractors
Job seekers have been complaining about Evolution Travel, its members and agents like Deidre Norton online and to the Better Business Bureau for years.

In 2021, Evolution Travel was among 1,000 companies put on notice by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission that they could face fines if they or their representatives made "misleading, or deceptive representations" about a "money-making opportunity."
Kovacic said a firm that "defied" FTC notices and continued to persist in these practices would be a "worthy target for an investigation."
CBC News found numerous complaints online about companies linked to the job postings. (Illustration: Matthew Hoddy/CBC, Reddit, Better Business Bureau)
Ron Archer, the CEO of Archer Travel Services, said that the company does "not condone illegal job postings and addresses them when we are made aware."
Yet in videos online, travel agents connected to Evolution Travel talked openly about using LinkedIn job postings to recruit people into the business.
Archer said they cannot "tell people how they train for their business" because they have "27,000 independent contractors around the world."
"LinkedIn is a big one," said one member in a June 2026 training video posted to YouTube. "We have quite a few different trainings on how to post on LinkedIn."
Jay Jones, who has gotten tens of thousands of jobs taken down from platforms himself, said companies like LinkedIn and Monster generate revenue through this traffic.

"There's no actual vetting of what companies get to be created, what jobs get to be listed," said Jones. "People coming [to LinkedIn] believing that there are real opportunities are greeted with this MLM nonsense."

articles.title: I studied silence in Ukraine, but moving to Montreal made me truly understand it
articles.summary: When Anna Lyhina moved from Ukraine to Quebec, she realized immigration can produce its own form of silence — not because anyone forbade her to speak. Learning a new language was about becoming…

image.caption: When Anna Lyhina moved from Ukraine to Montreal, she realized immigration can produce its own form of silence. (Submitted by Anna Lyhina)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person

When Anna Lyhina moved from Ukraine to Quebec, she realized immigration can produce its own form of silence — not because anyone forbade her to speak. Learning a new language was about becoming herself again.
For the first time in my life, I knew exactly what I wanted to say but could not say it
This First Person is the experience of Anna Lyhina, who lives in Montreal. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

I've always enjoyed spending more time immersed in literature than in the real world. The magic of reading is co-creation. A writer chooses what to say, but also what to leave unsaid. And each of us as readers fills those gaps with our own memories, fears, knowledge or prejudice.
Maybe that was why I became so interested in silence. Not as the absence of meaning, but the place where meaning takes its final shape.

I spent years studying silence as part of my PhD in Ukrainian literature. My thesis was about Hrytsko Chubai, an underground Ukrainian poet who wrote about things that could not always be said openly in a totalitarian state, but also about the limits of language itself and the things that words cannot fully express.

Then the war began between Russia and Ukraine. Many talented, strong people found their voices and spoke up through their journalism, human rights advocacy or writing. But I lost mine. I finally understood my grandmother's reaction when I would ask her about her experience during the Second World War. She always said it was bad but didn't elaborate. Not because she didn't remember. She said it was just hard to explain.
With the invasion of Russia, I felt the same. Words were no longer enough and I had nothing else. I didn't want to explore what that silence hid.
Shortly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Lyhina built a snowman armed with a stick with her dad. (Submitted by Anna Lyhina)

I just ran away from it, leaving my PhD with only four months left, and bought a one-way ticket to Montreal. At the time, I thought a major war in Europe was inevitable. It made little sense to me to build a life in Poland or Germany if Russian tanks might reach them in a few years. North America felt farther away, so Canada was a logical choice.
People often talk about immigration as a movement, but it felt more like disappearance.
I arrived in Montreal with one backpack, about $100 and no French.
For the first time in my life, I knew exactly what I wanted to say but could not say it.
People often describe learning a new language as learning new words. I experienced it as recovering my ability to exist socially.

items: Q&A: Lebanese-Canadian pens new memoir about finding belonging in a new country
What is driving young anglophones out of Que­bec?

blocks.text: At first, I could only communicate needs.
I need a SIM card.
I need a bank account.
I need an apartment.
I thought the problem was vocabulary.
It wasn't.
Lyhina in Montreal in 2024. She was interested in reading what people had scratched onto the metal railing at Mount Royal. (Submitted by Anna Lyhina)

I left the language in which I could think without effort. I left the people who understood my jokes before I finished them. I left my university and my work. The version of myself that other people knew disappeared. At home, I could shape how I was perceived through language — through intonation, word choice, the structure of a sentence. People could hear that I was educated, ironic, perhaps a little arrogant.
In a foreign language, I lost that control. I knew what I wanted to say, but not how to make it sound like me. Actually it wasn't a bad thing; it made me more sincere.
My humour was still there. My memories. My education. My way of thinking. My ability to write.
None of them had disappeared.
They had simply become inaccessible to everyone except me.

items: Chips vs. fries: I speak English fluently and yet I am always translating

blocks.text: Immigration changed my language. The silence came from what I believed that change meant.
So I postponed conversations. I rewrote simple messages over and over. I apologized before expressing an opinion. I waited until I could describe precisely to justify taking someone else's attention.
I believed I had to earn the right to speak again — and that started while I was volunteering with Montrealers experiencing homelessness.
People often asked me about my life. Much more rarely did they tell me about theirs, and I didn't ask because I didn't want to be intrusive.

items: I'm an Acadian at heart even if my accent marks me as an outsider

blocks.text: Then, months later, one person casually mentioned he used to repair airplanes in Moldova. Someone else had walked across half the country. Another wrote songs. One man had such an incredible memory for history that we spent hours playing the same game: he would tell me a fact, and I would check it out and get impressed.
I would ask why they had never told me before.
The answers were surprisingly familiar.
"I didn't think you'd be interested."
"I didn't think you'd care."
"I didn't think anyone would listen."
I was always surprised. Of course I wanted to hear it.
Then I suddenly recognized I had been saying exactly the same thing to myself. I thought I had nothing worth saying, so better I shut up and learn to communicate without mistakes first.
That day I understood something I never reached in my thesis.
Silence is not always the absence of words.
Sometimes it is the conviction that your words have no place in another person's world.

Sometimes that silence is imposed politically. But sometimes it is created by poverty. Sometimes people are simply misheard or ignored. Sometimes it comes from the language barrier. Sometimes it's created by our own fears.
Lyhina is learning who she is in a new language and city. In this case, she was trying to remember the word for apple in French. (Submitted by Anna Lyhina)
From outside it looks remarkably similar.

It took me a long time to understand that nobody was actually keeping me silent. I started speaking before I felt ready because there was no moment when the old version of me would suddenly return. My voice is something I have to use. And even if it's not perfect, I'm here now, in this version of me living in Canada.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anna Lyhina has a master's of literature from Kyiv-Mohyla Academy. She is a Ukrainian writer who came to Montreal from Kharkiv during the war.

articles.title: Montreal tenants without hot water, electricity during heated dispute over renovations
articles.summary: A group of private investors bought the units in 2024 under the banner Norgate Québec Inc. The Comité logement Saint-Laurent says many of the units are occupied by immigrants and recent newcomers to…

image.caption: Élodie Fortuné is trying to stop workers from entering her apartment and renovating her heating system. She has a sign on her door barring them from entry. (Sharon Yonan-Renold/CBC)

blocks.text: Élodie Fortuné has taped a note to her front door — and she's hoping it will stop workers from entering her apartment.
It reads, "The landlord has no legal authorization to enter or perform work here."
Fortuné's landlords want to change the heating system from centralized gas to electricity. But she believes that by doing so, the owners of the building would be changing the conditions of her lease.
Fortuné lives in one of the Norgate apartments, a grouping of more than 70 buildings along a stretch of Décarie Boulevard and Ouimet Street in Montreal's Saint-Laurent borough.
Her lease still says the owners cover the cost of hot water and heating, but once the heating system is renovated, all those expenses will end up on her hydro bill.
"My rent represents three-quarters of my budget," she says.
"If this work takes place ... so that when all is said and done I have exorbitant bills, what will I do?"
A Montreal landlord wants to replace 100s of tenants' heating systems. Here's why many are resisting

A group of private investors bought the units in 2024 under the name Norgate Québec Inc. The Comité logement Saint-Laurent, an organization that advocates for tenants' rights in the borough, says many of the units are occupied by immigrants and recent newcomers to Quebec.
In an email, a spokesperson for Norgate and the company that manages the buildings, Gestion Capital Montréal, says that the current heating and hot water systems are obsolete and need to be replaced.

"For leases that include heating and hot water, Norgate reimburses the additional Hydro-Québec electricity cost, based on a comparison with the same period the year before," says Nicolas Sima, with Gestion Capital Montréal.
The Norgate apartments include dozens of buildings along a stretch of Décarie Boulevard and Ouimet Street. (Sharon Yonan-Renold/CBC)
Tensions mounting between residents, new owners
CBC spoke to several residents who said they were concerned about the installation of the new heating system and the reimbursement structure.
Some residents are stopping workers from installing the new system in their apartments, with some even losing their hot water or heating in the process.
The Comité logement Saint-Laurent says many residents have lost trust in the new owners. This summer, dozens of tenants contested what they called excessive rent increases.

Maria Vasquez, the committee's general director, says she’s been helping roughly 200 Norgate residents who are resisting the heating changes. She says during lease renewals, the owners also tried to make residents responsible for all heating and hot water costs.
Maria Vasquez says that the owners are trying to force the residents to accept the changes. (Sharon Yonan-Renold/CBC)
She says while the owners are waiting for Quebec's housing board, the Tribunal administratif du logement (TAL) to rule on those cases, they shouldn't be carrying out the work.
"This is changing your contract, and this needs to be a tribunal decision," says Vasquez.
She argues that alternatively, the owners would need to reach an official agreement with tenants on the reimbursement structure.
Tenants alleging threats of steep penalties, utility cuts

Vasquez says that the buildings' managers are telling tenants that workers need to install individual water heaters and electric baseboards heaters, as they decommission the centralized system, saying that if workers aren't allowed in, tenants could lose access to heating and hot water.
In some cases, Vasquez says, building managers have threatened to charge residents $500 a day if workers are not allowed in.
"You see the intimidation here to make them to accept this," says Vasquez.
Fortuné adds that the building managers are also telling tenants that many of them will need to empty a closet to make room for the new water heaters, taking away crucial storage space.

items: Montreal landlords under fire for rent increases as high as 20% in Park Ex

blocks.text: Sima denies that the owners are intimidating tenants. He argues that they aren't changing the conditions of people's leases, so the company doesn't need approval from the TAL to carry out the work.
Sima adds that when a resident has been duly notified of the work and still doesn’t allow access to their unit, the company may seek to recover damages.
"To be able to claim them, we must mention them in our formal notices and in our applications to the Tribunal administratif du logement," he explains.
Sima says that the management company is offering to install a cabinet or shelving to make up for the lost storage. Still, Fortuné says that won't change the square footage of her apartment.
Grey area in the law
According to housing lawyer David Searle, what the law says on the topic isn't exactly black and white.
He says that tenants do have the option to contest major work, within 10 days of being notified. He says otherwise, tenants must allow building owners to carry out work in their units.
Searle says if tenants believe their landlord is not respecting the conditions of their lease, they can ask the TAL to intervene, but the board might not be able to stop the work from happening.

items: Housing project aims to give young Montrealers aging out of youth protection a home

blocks.text: "It would require research to look into how this specific situation has been treated before," explains Searle.

"On the one hand, one can understand where they're coming from. They have this expectation of a lease being breached. On the other hand, one can also expect that if they complain about their lack of heating [or hot water] they're going to be confronted with their own lack of collaboration," he says.

But the Coalition of Housing Committees and Tenants Associations of Quebec (RCLALQ) says residents are right to be upset over the proposed reimbursement system. Community organizer Jean-Christophe Bureau argues that it creates a power imbalance.
"If the renter isn't happy or does not reach the same calculation as the owner, the owner has the power to reimburse them or not," says Bureau.

items: Montreal wants rent control, mandatory registry. What would that look like?

blocks.text: Fortuné says that the stress of the situation is weighing heavily on her.
"This is the first time in the 16 years I've been in Quebec that I've had this knot in my stomach," she says.
She says she'll keep fighting for her rights as a tenant and to maintain her lease conditions.
"If the idea is to change the terms in a way that ends up increasing my rent even further — well, no."

articles.title: Anthropic IPO to test the first 'pure play' AI stock in a choppy market
articles.summary: American AI giant Anthropic's expected debut on the Nasdaq has one money manager recalling the dot-com bubble of the 2000s.

image.caption: Anthropic is one of the leading developers of generative AI models, competing with companies including OpenAI, Google and Meta. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: Anthropic's stock market debut is set to be big — a big valuation, big spending, big warnings, big uncertainty for investors and a big potential indicator of how the recently volatile artificial intelligence sector will fare in 2027.

In an amended U.S. regulatory filing Tuesday, San Francisco-based Anthropic set an expected initial public offering (IPO) price range of $70 US to $78 US per share. That implies a fully diluted market valuation of roughly $1.3 trillion US at the midpoint, climbing to $1.4 trillion US at the top end, marking the largest technology stock market debut on record.
"It's going to be one of the biggest IPOs in history," said Greg Taylor, portfolio manager at Vancouver-based PenderFund Capital Management.

The size of an IPO is typically measured by the amount of capital raised. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion US directly through its public share offering. If that happens, it will rank behind only SpaceX's record-setting stock market launch in June.

Taylor expects Anthropic shares will start trading before America celebrates Thanksgiving, on Nov. 26. Wealthsimple, the popular Canadian financial trading app, lists an expected "IPO day" of Nov. 30.
Ernest Wong, head of research at Toronto-based Baskin Wealth Management, anticipates the stock will be a serious heavyweight when it starts trading on the Nasdaq exchange.
"There are only a handful of stocks in the world that are valued over $1 trillion US," he said. "It speaks to how big AI really is."
What the CEO cheating scandal could mean for Nvidia and AI
What is Anthropic?
Anthropic started as a niche AI research lab in 2021, when its founders left rival OpenAI because they felt it was too focused on profits, ignoring risks and giving too much control to investors.
The company gained momentum in 2024, when it released Claude 3.5 Sonnet. This version beat OpenAI's GPT-4o on major performance benchmarks at a fraction of the cost of previous frontier AI models.

items: OpenAI scraps release of new AI model over safety concerns
BMO, CIBC, RBC, TD Bank block personal AI agents, citing safety and security
Will Anthropic's IPO go boom or bust?

blocks.text: Unlike Apple or Microsoft, Anthropic is not a traditional for-profit company. It's organized as a public benefit corporation, meaning its board has a legal mandate to balance public safety against maximizing shareholder returns.
Today, Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei is a leading advocate for AI safety, arguing the industry should slow development to let safety measures catch up.
In Anthropic's recent regulatory filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 94 of more than 300 pages were dedicated to spelling out a long list of risk factors.
"Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed," the company stated.

Anthropic says this may include, "behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model's continued operation," as well as actions that "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."
Big numbers
$1.4 trillion US is not the only eyebrow-raising figure associated with Anthropic's IPO.

The company's valuation has fluctuated wildly in recent months. $2 trillion US was recently on the table. In late May, private investors valued the company at $965 billion US, up from $380 billion US in February.
"There's a fairly big degree of optimism baked into these valuations as they're coming out," Taylor said.
"I don't think anyone can tell you what Anthropic is gonna look like five years out."
Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January 2025. (Markus Schreiber/The Associated Press)

The company's sales have been brisk. According to regulatory filings, Anthropic earned more than three and a half times as much revenue in the first six months of 2026 as it did in the entire previous calendar year. Roughly 20 per cent of those sales came from two big unnamed customers.

At the same time, the AI giant has been spilling a lot of red ink. It booked a $80.7 billion US net loss this year through June, although this was mainly due to non-cash accounting charges. The company lost $42 billion US in 2025.

Anthropic also has big spending plans. The company does not build or own physical data centres. Instead, it rents high-performance computing power from cloud providers like Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud through massive multi-year service contracts.

According to regulatory filings, Anthropic has locked in nearly $900 billion US in cloud and computing deals that run through the 2030s and 2040s. Partners in these deals include Broadcom, SpaceX AI, Google Cloud, Amazon Web Services, and Microsoft Azure.
A blockbuster IPO
Anthropic's IPO isn't noteworthy for its massive size alone.
"Buying the Anthropic IPO is one of the first pure play AI investments out there," Taylor said.

Until now, investors looking to own a piece of the artificial intelligence boom have been mainly limited to far less AI-focused technology stocks such as Microsoft or Nvidia, which makes chips. Google, for example, is widely-considered part of the AI investment theme. But the company also has massive businesses unrelated to AI, like its Android smartphones, and YouTube.

"The only thing they do is create new AI models," Wong said of Anthropic. "It's certainly a missing piece of the puzzle, in the sense that you have the public company data from all of the various players that are involved in AI, except for the model companies, which are largely Anthropic and OpenAI."
If Anthropic's IPO is seen as a new benchmark for AI investment, its first trading sessions will come amid significant volatility for the technology sector.

Earlier this month, tech and AI stocks experienced sharp sell-offs and swift rebounds as markets entered correction territory. This was due in part to concerns about AI companies matching their big spending with sufficient profits. The situation was compounded by political concerns in the U.S. after the midterms about tighter regulation for AI and data centres.

At the same time, the recent scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy adds a new dimension to AI investment concerns. The chipmaker's stock, seen as a bellwether for the AI trade, has erased billions in market capitalization in recent days on the Nasdaq, where Anthropic is set to debut.
Like the dot com bubble?

"The main risk for Anthropic is that essentially they have to compete with other model providers. It's a very competitive market," Wong said. "OpenAI makes their own models. SpaceX through Grok is a leading model lab. Certainly, Google and Meta are competing in this space."
He predicts the stock won't be for the faint of heart early on, as investors rank each new Anthropic product against peers and evaluate it's huge spending on data services.
"It'll be very volatile," Wong said.
Such has been the case with SpaceX since its Nasdaq debut in June. The stock surged about 19 per cent on day one. Since then, it's dipped as much as 22 per cent below its $135 US IPO price.

For Taylor, the AI sector's massive spending, blistering stock run-ups and tight business links between a handful of tech companies are all reminders of a previous investment frenzy that separated winners from losers in spectacular fashion.
"The dot-com bubble is certainly the one that's probably most real in a lot of people's minds," he said. "Everyone wanted a piece of the internet back in 2000."
While companies like Pets.com went bust, Google and Microsoft became household names.
"There's a lot of big parallels here with AI," Taylor said. "It's just figuring out who's going to win at the end of the day."

articles.title: American Airlines resumes flights to Haiti, providing a vital route into the country
articles.summary: The U.S. airline has begun flying into northern Haiti on a daily basis, providing a vital route into the country at a time when Americans have few options to get there as the U.S. government advises…

image.caption: Haitian and U.S. flags are displayed at the front of an American Airlines flight that landed in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti on Nov. 1. It was the U.S. air carrier's first flight to the country since service was suspended in late 2024. (Gérard Maxineau/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. airline has begun flying into northern Haiti on a daily basis, providing a vital route into the country at a time when Americans have few options to get there as the U.S. government advises people to avoid all travel to the Caribbean nation due to security concerns.
Airline resumes service to northern city of Cap-Haïtien amid U.S. State Department's security concerns

A major U.S. airline has begun flying into northern Haiti on a daily basis, providing a vital route into the country at a time when Americans have few options to get there amid U.S. government advice to avoid all travel to the Caribbean nation due to security concerns.

At the start of November, American Airlines relaunched daily non-stop service from Miami to the port city of Cap-Haïtien after a years-long absence that began during the pandemic and persisted through a prolonged period of instability that has followed in Haiti.
"We are ​excited ​to return ​to Haiti," the airline told CBC News via email, pointing to the important link the route provides between the two countries.

Yet the route is resuming at a time when the U.S. State Department is advising people not to travel to Haiti for any reason, as a result of the ongoing state of emergency in the country and general security risks — including crime, kidnapping and unrest. Canada's government is also currently warning people not to visit the country.

Haiti has endured a series of crises, including years of political chaos, widespread gang violence and a related wave of civilian displacement. The country also faces major challenges with hunger at the moment.

The State Department nonetheless sees value in Americans having another way to get to Haiti, telling CBC News that it "welcomes" the airline's new service to Cap-Haïtien — even though its travel advice is unchanged.
"The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," the State Department said.
A 'very complicated' journey lately
The return of the American Airlines service between South Florida and the western side of the island of Hispaniola, is likewise welcomed by members of the Haitian community in the U.S.

Wolf Pamphile, the founder and CEO of Haiti Policy House, a Washington, D.C.,-based think-tank, said travel to Haiti has been "very complicated" for those trying to get there from the U.S. — with Haitian carrier Sunrise Airways being one of the main options.
LISTEN | The Trump administration and Haiti:
Front Burner36:28Why is Trump so focused on Haiti?

The United States has a large Haitian diaspora, particularly in Florida. But Pamphile said there are also many people with ties to Haiti living in parts of the northeastern U.S. — including in New York, New Jersey and Massachusetts.
He says the return of American Airlines to Cap-Haïtien gives Haiti-bound American air travellers more reliability and a level of customer service "that doesn't exist in the market right now."
For Florida resident Gilson Morusuma, American Airlines' re-entry into the Haitian market brings the prospect of better service and more competitive pricing for air travel to his home country.

But when speaking to The Haitian Times, he noted that while the return of the American Airlines route offers travellers like himself a new option, "it does not resolve the broader challenges facing the country's aviation sector or restore service to the capital."
Shift in air traffic

Pamphile says the security situation in Haiti's capital of Port-au-Prince has led to a shift in air traffic, to the point where Cap-Haïtien has become "the main hub" for many international flights to the island.
Pamphile noted that while Port-au-Prince faces gang-related security challenges, the situation is "drastically different" in Cap-Haïtien, which is about 200 kilometres north of the capital.
Pilots watch the runway from the cockpit of a plane landing in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, in April 2026. (Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty Images)

Regarding security considerations surrounding its flights to Cap-Haïtien, American Airlines told CBC News it "conducts ​a comprehensive ​review ​of a variety ​of operational, safety and ​business ​considerations before ​starting service."

There were a spate of publicly reported incidents in November 2024 of gangs firing at aircraft in Port-au-Prince — including an American Airlines flight. As a result, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration banned U.S. flights from landing in the capital — a ban that's been extended into 2027.

The November 2024 incidents also led to a shutdown of the international airport in Port-au-Prince. Seven months after, Haiti's Sunrise airline operated the first commercial flight out of the capital, according to The Associated Press.
Fellow U.S. carrier JetBlue Airways used to fly to Haiti, but halted service in 2024 after one of its planes was shot at when departing Port-au-Prince.
In July, JetBlue president Marty St. George told the Miami Herald the airline had no plans to return.
JetBlue told CBC News it did not have "any updates or additional information to share regarding our service to Haiti."
Parallel advice from Ottawa
Like its U.S. counterpart, Global Affairs Canada is also telling travellers to avoid all travel to Haiti given the "extremely volatile" security situation in the country.
As such, two Canadian airlines that previously flew to Haiti have no immediate plans to restart flights to the country.

"We do not anticipate resuming our service to Port-au-Prince in the near future," Stéphanie Dussault, an Air Transat spokesperson, told CBC News via email. "We continue to assess the situation in Haiti, with the safety of our passengers and crew guiding any decision about future service."
That's also the case at Air Canada, which is not operating flights to Haiti at this time.
"We continue to closely monitor the situation and will assess opportunities to resume service when conditions allow," Yasmine Mehdi, an airline spokesperson, said in an emailed statement.

articles.title: Bundeswehr study exposes widespread sexual harassment in German military
articles.summary: Sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known, with younger women disproportionately affected. Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has called for a policy of "zero…

image.caption: For the first time, a study on unreported cases provides reliable data on sexual misconduct in the German Armed ForcesImage: Florian Gaertner/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag on Wednesday. Earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defence Committee.

According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known. "The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius said, announcing an action plan to address the issue. "There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr."
Women in Germany's military suffer widespread sexual abuse — study
Many victims stay silent

The study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. To this end, the Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are scientifically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.
Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Some 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers said they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment. 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct. 2% of both women and men said they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was a desire not to draw attention to themselves. "There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive issue is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.
Why Germany struggles to recruit women soldiers
Greens call for independent reporting office for victims

In response, the Bundeswehr plans to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism. Defence policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfil their responsibilities.

Another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction. "Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," said Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defence Minister Pistorius stressed.
Germany rearms, but who will serve in the military?
Reported cases on the rise

The study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

The current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he said, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defence must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice."

The Bundeswehr is in urgent need of additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘Tourists hate themselves’ – which is why Tasmania is telling people to stay away
articles.summary:
Island state declares it ‘is not really for tourists’ – but is the marketing strategy just a cheeky piece of reverse psychology?

  • Get our

blocks.text: Research shows “tourists hate themselves” – which is exactly why the marketing flacks at Tourism Tasmania are telling them to stay away from the island state.

Its new campaign declares the island state is “not really for tourists”, enlisting former SBS newsreader Lee Lin Chin to help sell the tongue-in-cheek campaign, based on the idea that Australians prefer identifying as a “traveller” rather than a “tourist”.
Its centrepiece is a short video of a man being pointed to the back of an endless queue for a “world famous” pastry. He eventually abandons the line to find solitude in the Tasmanian outdoors.
Chin, who lives mostly offline without a mobile phone, also fronts videos exploring the walking trails on her visit.
Tourism Tasmania’s CEO, Sarah Kingston Clark, said the campaign was deliberately wry rather than anti-visitor, to reflect the “tensions” of modern travel.
Those tensions play out in the research, Prof Can-Seng Ooi, the professor of cultural and heritage tourism at the University of Tasmania, suggested.

blocks.caption: ‘Instead of the cold north, we are talking about the cold south … it’s a quiet place, time slows down,’ says Prof Can-Seng Ooi. Photograph: Tourism Tasmania

blocks.text: “Studies have shown that tourists hate themselves,” he said. “They want to avoid each other.”
after newsletter promotion
Ooi identified stressed people yearning for “quietness” as the campaign’s target audience, especially those living in urban cities on the mainland.
“It taps into the type of tourist people want to be,” Ooi said. He added that people prefer to view themselves as “travellers” because of the negative connotation of “tourist”.
Ooi spent 20 years living in Scandinavia, researching how tourism, culture and heritage contributes to the development of regional destinations.

“The message is very Scandinavian, even the imagery: the sauna, the vinyl records, the books and so on,” Ooi said. “Instead of the cold north, we are talking about the cold south … it’s a quiet place, time slows down.”

Char-lee McLennan, an associate professor from QUT’s school of management, said the campaign used “an element of reverse psychology” that could benefit regional economies by steering visitors beyond established hotspots.
Prof David Waller, a marketing expert with UTS, said Tasmania’s “Come down for air” theme was less “anti-tourist” and “more anti-overcrowded, line-joining, tourist destinations”.
“Lee Lin Chin is adding humour to the message,” he said. “Lee Lin Chin is an icon – intelligent, avant garde and [she has a] dry sense of humour.”

But, McLennan said, the campaign’s success depends on whether the real experience of visiting Tasmania lives up to its promise as well as delivering meaningful economic benefits to regional communities.

articles.title: Ugandan police investigate deaths of four pupils in suspected school poisoning
articles.summary: The head teacher of the school has been arrested to assist police investigations.

blocks.text: Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.
The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.
The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.
According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.
Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.
Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.
A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.
The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.
Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.
The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.
The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.
Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.
The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

articles.title: Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds
articles.summary: Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

blocks.text: High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores faced no such penalty. In one group, they were treated better.
The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them, and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, the researcher behind the study, Nitya Chawla, says, women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.
How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Help and mistreatment were reported by the participants themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity. In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.
IQ 130 = Genius? The truth about IQ tests
Why are intelligent women seen as hostile at work?

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.
"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.
Do men with high intelligence scores face the same treatment?
No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.
Should women hide their intelligence at work?
No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.
What can managers do about gender bias at work?

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should keep track of how members of their teams treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.
Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

articles.title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to…

blocks.text: Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.

Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.

blocks.text: In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair

blocks.caption: US intelligence officials  had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang. Photograph: CTI/AFPTV/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.

US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.

Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.

The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …
Who is Alice Huang?

Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.

There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.

Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.
What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?

The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”

Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).

“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.

China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”
“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.
What approach has the US taken?

Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.

But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for ovarian cancer, a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread. Photograph: Simon Dawson/PA

blocks.text: Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.
The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

Modi's Hindu nationalist government has long sought to emphasize India's pre-colonial cultural identity
Image: Mayank Makhija/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: What you need to know
Here is our rolling coverage from India on Thursday, November 12:

items: India's cabinet has passed plans to develop the 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' showcasing India's civilization journey
Two colonial-era blocks in Central Delhi, that earlier as government offices, are being transformed to house the museum
The first gallery under the project is expected to open next year

blocks.text: November 12, 2026
Mega museum on Indian civilization gets cabinet nod

blocks.caption: The first part of the large museum is expected to open up next yearImage: Sonu Mehta/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has approved the development of a massive museum in the heart of India's capital, New Delhi, estimated to cost around $340 million (around €306 million).
The 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' — which was first announced by Modi in 2023 — is being billed as the museum "with the largest display area in the world."

The Sanskrit name of the museum translates to 'India through the ages'. The project has been envisaged as the country's landmark museum, the government said, and will showcase elements of Indian history and civilization, which spans thousands of years.
Modi hails 'timeless richness' of Indian civilization
The century-old North and South Blocks in New Delhi's Raisina Hills — the seat of the Indian government — will be reused for the museum.

The colonial-era twin blocks once housed government offices, including Modi's own, before they were vacated over the last year as part of the Modi government's redesigning of India's hub of political power.
The Hindu nationalist government has long sought to emphasize India's pre-colonial cultural identity.

"Buildings that have been centres of governance will now become a place where millions can discover, experience and celebrate the timeless richness of our civilisation," Modi wrote on X on Wednesday night.

Calling the museum a "magnificent celebration" of India's "civilizational journey", Modi said the museum's galleries will bring to life aspects including ancient knowledge systems, mathematics, astronomy to architecture, art, languages and spirituality, through "immersive experiences."
Inaugural gallery to open in 2027
According to a press release from the Indian cabinet, the museum will encompass an area of nearly 178,509 square meters with the ability to welcome some 10 million visitors a year.

The finalization of the project isn't planned until 2030/31, but the first gallery on the theme of "adornment" will open its doors to the public next year, with more galleries gradually opening after that.

The content and collection analysis for the museum is currently underway, with the government having identified some 1.8 million objects for possible display from national and state museums, alongside archaeological and private collections.
